passage: Lalremsiami had been waiting for weeks to beat her cousin Shalini at cricket in the colony lane. Shalini's marks in maths were higher, and Lalremsiami wanted that to change. In the game she bowled her best over, and Shalini hit a boundary anyway. Lalremsiami felt a hot flash and thought, I want her to miss. She stopped, took a breath and noticed that this was too much. Then she asked, "How do you keep your wrist so still?" Shalini showed her. The next ball, Lalremsiami got her out. They both laughed. At homework time she asked Shalini to explain the maths trick too.

qa.q: Whose marks in maths were higher?
qa.a: Shalini's marks in maths were higher.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she thought, "I want her to miss"?
qa.a: She felt a hot rush of rivalry and jealousy, wanting her cousin to fail, and then realised it was more than friendly competition.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do next that turned the rivalry into something useful?
qa.a: She asked Shalini how she keeps her wrist still and later asked her to explain the maths trick, so she learned from her cousin's strengths.

qa.q: How might Shalini have seen Lalremsiami's question about her wrist?
qa.a: Shalini probably felt respected and pleased to be asked, which made the game friendlier for her too.

grounding: A child wants to beat her cousin at cricket and studies, notices when rivalry becomes wanting her to lose, and chooses to enjoy and learn from her.

passage:
From Nani's holiday notebook, Tuesday.
Pankaj and Nikita played cricket in the courtyard all afternoon. Pankaj kept count loudly: 'Twenty-three runs to your eleven!' When Nikita hit a six over the tulsi, he claimed it was out. Later, doing holiday homework, he kept peeking at her page and racing to finish first. Tonight he sulked because she knew the capital of Peru and he didn't. I called him into the kitchen. 'Do you want to play with Nikita, or beat her?' He thought, then said, 'Both. But mostly beat.' I asked him what she does well. 'She bowls spin better than me,' he admitted. Tomorrow he has asked her to teach him the googly. I'll watch how it goes.

qa.q: What did Nikita know that Pankaj didn't?
Why did Pankaj claim Nikita's six was out?
qa.a: He felt threatened and jealous, wanting so badly to be better that he couldn't bear her doing well.

qa.q: What question from Nani helped Pankaj, and what did he decide?
qa.a: 'Do you want to play with Nikita, or beat her?'; he decided to ask her to teach him the googly.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel when her six was called out?
qa.a: Annoyed and unfairly treated, since the six was a good hit.

grounding: A grandmother's notebook shows a boy's rivalry with his cousin turning unfair, and a question that turns it towards learning from her.

passage:
Sunday
Dear diary, Darshan writing. Jasleen came for the weekend again, and I spent the whole time trying to beat her. Swimming race at the club: she won by a whole arm. Then Chachi asked about the maths olympiad, and Jasleen had a gold certificate and I had silver. I went quiet all through dinner. Tonight I noticed something ugly. When Jasleen dropped her ice cream, I was glad. Glad! That's not who I want to be. It's fine to want to be good, but wanting her to fall is something else. Tomorrow I'm going to ask how she learnt that flip turn at the wall. Maybe if I learn from her instead of racing her every second, I'll actually get faster.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel on noticing the gladness about the dropped ice cream?
qa.a: Ashamed and uneasy, seeing that the rivalry had turned into wanting Jasleen to fail.

qa.q: What plan does Darshan make for tomorrow?
qa.a: To ask Jasleen how she learnt her flip turn, learning from her instead of racing her every second.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Darshan's quiet dinner?
qa.a: She might feel confused or uneasy, unsure why her gold certificate made her cousin go silent.

grounding: A child writes about a rivalry with a cousin, notices wanting her to fail, and decides to learn from her strengths.
